quiz.q: What does a language model produce at each step?
options: A probability for every possible next token
quiz.why: It scores every token in its vocabulary. A sampler picks one, appends it, and the loop runs again.

quiz.q: What does raising the temperature do?
options: Flattens the odds, so less likely tokens get picked more often
quiz.why: Temperature divides the scores before softmax. Above 1 the distribution flattens; near 0 the top token almost always wins.

quiz.q: Why can a model struggle to count the letters in a word?
options: It sees tokens, often whole chunks of a word, not single letters
It has no memory at all
quiz.why: A word like "strawberry" may be one or two tokens, so the individual letters are never directly in front of the model.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, using the chain rule
quiz.why: It works backward from the loss, multiplying local derivatives, so every weight learns which direction lowers the loss.

quiz.q: Your loss jumps around and then shoots up. What's the likely cause?
quiz.why: Steps that are too big overshoot the bottom of the valley and can bounce out of it entirely.

quiz.q: Why do networks need a nonlinear activation like tanh or ReLU?
options: Without one, stacked layers collapse into a single linear function
quiz.why: A chain of linear maps is still a linear map. Nonlinearity is what lets a network bend its decision boundary.

quiz.q: In self-attention, what does each token do?
options: Gathers information from other tokens, weighted by how relevant they are
quiz.why: Each token's query is compared with every key; the scores become weights for mixing the values.

quiz.q: Why does a GPT-style model mask out future tokens?
options: So training matches generation, where the future isn't known yet
quiz.why: With a causal mask, every position learns to predict the next token from only what came before.

quiz.q: GPT models are which kind of transformer?
quiz.why: They are stacks of masked self-attention blocks that predict the next token.

quiz.q: About how much memory do the weights of an 8B model take at Q4_K_M (about 4.85 bits per weight)?
quiz.why: 8 billion x 4.85 bits / 8 = about 4.85 GB, before the KV cache and overhead.

quiz.q: What usually limits how fast a local model writes tokens?
options: Memory bandwidth, because every token reads all the active weights
quiz.why: Generating one token streams the weights through the chip, so bytes per second sets the ceiling.

quiz.q: What's the catch with a mixture-of-experts model like Qwen3-30B-A3B?
options: It's fast like a 3B model, but all 30B weights still need to fit in memory
quiz.why: Only a few experts run per token, which helps speed, but any expert might be picked, so all of them stay loaded.

quiz.q: In a coding agent, what usually ends the loop?
options: The model replies without asking for a tool
quiz.why: Each turn, the harness runs any tool calls and sends the results back. When the model answers with plain text, the task is done.

quiz.q: What is context compaction?
options: Replacing older messages with a shorter summary so the run fits the context window
quiz.why: Long runs pile up tool output. Summarizing old turns frees room while keeping what matters.

quiz.q: Which part actually edits files on your computer?
options: The harness, when it runs the tool call the model asked for
quiz.why: The model only writes text, such as a request to call edit with some arguments. The harness executes it.

quiz.q: The usual rule for printing overhangs without support is...
options: Up to about 45 degrees from vertical
quiz.why: Past about 45 degrees each new layer has too little of the layer below to sit on, so it droops.

quiz.q: Halving the layer height does what to print time, roughly?
quiz.why: Twice as many layers, each taking about as long, means about twice the time.

quiz.q: Why can't a 0.4 mm nozzle print a 0.1 mm wall?
options: A single extruded line is about as wide as the nozzle, so walls come in steps near that width
quiz.why: One line is roughly 0.4 to 0.45 mm wide. Thinner features get dropped or printed too thick.

tracks.title: The math under AI
tracks.blurb: Just enough linear algebra, calculus and probability to read any AI paper without fear.

steps.note: Vectors: arrows, lists of numbers, and why both views matter.
Matrix multiplication is doing one transformation after another. This is every layer of a network.
Derivatives without the dread.
Gradient descent, one small step at a time.
Bayes' theorem as geometry: how evidence should change your beliefs.
SVD: the matrix factorization behind compression, PCA and LoRA.

quiz.q: A neural network layer mostly does what to its input vector?
options: Multiplies it by a matrix, adds a bias, then applies a nonlinearity
quiz.why: That's the core of a dense layer: a linear transformation followed by an activation.

quiz.q: The gradient of the loss points...
options: In the direction the loss increases fastest
quiz.why: So training steps the opposite way, downhill.

quiz.q: What does LoRA use that SVD also shows?
options: Big matrices can often be approximated by products of much thinner ones
quiz.why: LoRA learns a low-rank update, two thin matrices, instead of changing the full weight matrix.

steps.title: FlashAttention (paper)
steps.note: The classic example of making attention fast by respecting the memory hierarchy.

quiz.q: Why are GPUs good at neural networks?
options: Thousands of simple cores do the same math on many numbers at once, which is what matrix multiplication needs
quiz.why: Matrix multiplication is massively parallel, which is exactly the shape of GPU hardware.

quiz.q: What does FlashAttention avoid?
options: Writing the full attention matrix to slow GPU memory, by working in tiles in fast on-chip memory
quiz.why: Attention is often limited by memory traffic, not math. Tiling keeps the work in fast SRAM.
